sections.content: How many people stayed in New Mills after gaining qualifications?

New Mills is a small town in the East Midlands. New Mills does not have its own university.

New Mills has lower levels of deprivation.

Overall, New Mills ended up with:

  • fewer graduates than it produced
  • a similar number of non-graduates with advanced qualifications as it produced
Note: all towns and cities in this analysis are defined based on population size only. This means that some cities are classed as towns because of their population.

Let's explore this further

There were 600 state-school pupils from New Mills who sat their GCSEs between the 2007 to 2008 and the 2010 to 2011 school years.

Of these, 195 (33%) went on to gain degree-level qualifications (level 6+ as defined by The Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation, or Ofqual ). We will call these people graduates.

Another 190 (32%) went on to gain other advanced post-16 qualifications, such as A-Levels, a foundation degree or higher apprenticeship (levels 3-5 as defined by Ofqual). In this tool, we will refer to these non-graduates with advanced qualifications as “qualified non-graduates", for brevity.

The charts below compare New Mills to other English towns and cities using three measures:

  • what proportion of New Mills' pupils became graduates or qualified non-graduates by the 2017 to 2018 academic year
  • of those graduates and qualified non-graduates, the percentages that lived in New Mills in the 2018 to 2019 academic year
  • how many graduates and qualified non-graduates from elsewhere came to live there by 2018 to 2019, relative to the number who sat their GCSEs there

In some towns, some of this information may not be available because of small sample sizes.
The size and deprivation level of a town, as well as the qualification levels of older residents, were all related to students' educational attainment. Read our previous analysis.

Where did those who left New Mills move to?

Of New Mills's graduates, 85 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 30 of those graduates (35%) were living fairly locally, in the Manchester travel to work area (TTWA).

Of New Mills's qualified (level 3+) non-graduates, 65 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 35 of those qualified non-graduates (54%) were living fairly locally, in the Manchester travel to work area (TTWA).

Of those in New Mills' GCSE cohort:

  • 75 graduates left the East Midlands
  • the most common region they moved to was the North West
  • 40 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates left the East Midlands
  • the most common region they moved to was the North West

In 2018 to 2019, 36% of graduates and 29% of qualified non-graduates living in New Mills had moved there from elsewhere

In the 2018 to 2019 academic year, there were 165 graduates and 175 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates from our cohort living in New Mills. This is compared with the 195 graduates and 190 qualified non-graduates who had lived there when they sat their GCSEs.

In 2018 to 2019, 64% of the graduates had also lived in New Mills as GCSE pupils, while 36% had moved there from elsewhere.

Of the qualified non-graduates who lived in New Mills in 2018 to 2019, 71% had lived there as GCSE pupils, while 29% had moved to the area from elsewhere.
